text: The word kuvāri⟨NOTE:44⟩ in general means a man who is extremely selfish, miserly, performs no sacrifice and leads a contemptible life. In the present ṛk, where akavārim stands, the word kava means a small, despised person, and the compound is kava-ari: a petty enemy. One who is not a kavāri is an akavāri, that is, an enemy of great power; or an abundant number may also be indicated by it. It is an epithet showing Indra's greatness: one who can face such enemies.

text: This is the tenth sūkta of the fourth anuvāka, सद्यो ह (*sadyo ha*), of five ṛks; the seer is Viśvāmitra, the deity Indra, the metre Triṣṭubh. The Anukramaṇikā begins सद्यो ह (*sadyo ha*). Uses: in the Agniṣṭoma, at the midday pressing, this sūkta (सद्यो ह जात (*sadyo ha jāta*)) belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa śastra, and the sūtra says सद्यो ह जात एवा त्वामिंद्र (*sadyo ha jāta evā tvāmiṃdra*) (Ā. Sū. 5.16).⟨NOTE:45⟩ On the Cāturviṃśika day, in the Maitrāvaruṇa śastra, this sūkta is the one called ahar-ahaḥ-śasya; the sūtra says सद्यो ह जात इत्यहरहःशस्यं मैत्रावरुणः (*sadyo ha jāta ityaharahaḥśasyaṃ maitrāvaruṇaḥ*) (Ā. Sū. 7.4). In an ahargaṇa, from the second day onward, at the midday pressing, it is used in this śastra; the sūtra: अहरहः शस्यानीति होत्रका द्वितीयादिष्टेव (*aharahaḥ śasyānīti hotrakā dvitīyādiṣṭeva*) (Ā. Sū. 7.1). In the one-day sādyaskra rite, in the Marutvatīya śastra, its first ṛk सद्यो ह जात (*sadyo ha jāta*) is the sūktamukhīya (opening verse); the sūtra: सद्यो ह जातो वृषभः कनीनस्त्वं सद्यो अपिबो जात इंद्र । (*sadyo ha jāto vṛṣabhaḥ kanīnastvaṃ sadyo apibo jāta iṃdra |*) (Ā. Sū. 9.5).

text: O Indra, on the day on which you were born, on that very day, when the desire for this Soma arose, you drank the nectar, the fresh juice, of the अंशोः (*aṃśoḥ*), which is distinguished by pieces of the Soma plant, of the ṛjīṣa, गिरिष्ठां (*giriṣṭhāṃ*) (गिरिस्थां (*giristhāṃ*)), standing on the high place of a mountain.⟨NOTE:46⟩ He shows the reason for drinking Soma at the very moment of birth: your mother (जनित्री (*janitrī*)), the young woman (योषा (*yoṣā*)) Aditi, in the lying-in chamber of your great father, your begetter Kaśyapa (महः पितुः दमे (*mahaḥ pituḥ dame*)), before giving the breast (अग्रे (*agre*)), poured that Soma around you (पर्यासिंचत् (*paryāsiṃcat*)), that is, made it flow all around your mouth.

text: Pṛtanās are battles, where warriors engage. In them Indra is स्वराजं (*svarājaṃ*), self-ruling; हरिष्ठां (*hariṣṭhāṃ*) is हरिस्थां (*haristhāṃ*), standing in a chariot yoked with bay horses; नृतमं (*nṛtamaṃ*) is the best leader of strength in battle; द्विता (*dvitā*) means that, having come to battle, he proceeds dividing the enemy army in two. No one at all surpasses (तरति (*tarati*)) this Indra; the sense is that no one equals him. नु (*nu*) is a particle of well-known fact. That Indra, इनतमः (*inatamaḥ*), the greatest lord of the army, goes with the Maruts, the सत्वभिः (*satvabhiḥ*), who sit round about him. With his शूषैः (*śūṣaiḥ*), strengths that dry up (shoṣayanti) the forces of the foe, and being पृथुज्रयाः (*pṛthujrayāḥ*), of intense speed toward battle, he destroys the life, or the food, of the Dasyu, the enemy; ह (*ha*) is a particle of well-known fact. Sāyaṇa cites the Nirukta here, which explains पृथुज्रयाः (*pṛthujrayāḥ*) as पृथुजवः (*pṛthujavaḥ*) and then quotes the pāda of the ṛk, with a further word that is not clear (Ni. 5-9). ⟨NOTE:48⟩

text: That Indra is mighty, and in the pṛtanās, the battles, he is तरणिः (*taraṇiḥ*): he moves on having crossed over his enemies. The illustration is अर्वा न (*arvā na*): as a strong horse crosses the force of the enemy, so he pervades (व्यानशिः (*vyānaśiḥ*)) heaven and earth, the two रोदसी (*rodasī*). He is मेहनावान् (*mehanāvān*): mehana is wealth, which is poured out and given to those who ask, and he possesses it. Such an Indra, in the कारे (*kāre*), that is the sacrifice and the like (what is done, kriyate), is like Bhaga, the god Pūṣan, to be invoked (हव्यः (*havyaḥ*)); he is the protector of the praisers or of the praises (मतीनां (*matīnāṃ*)), like a father; lovely (चारुः (*cāruḥ*)); possessed of a good invocation (सुहवः (*suhavaḥ*)); and giver of food (वयोधा (*vayodhā*)). ⟨NOTE:50⟩

text: The sūkta beginning चर्षणीधृतं (*carṣaṇīdhṛtaṃ*) has twelve Ṛks and is Vaiśvāmitra (its seer is Viśvāmitra) and Aindra (its deity is Indra). The Anukramaṇikā says: चर्षणीधृतं द्वादशाद्यांत्यौ तृचौ जागतगायत्राविति (*carṣaṇīdhṛtaṃ dvādaśādyāṃtyau tṛcau jāgatagāyatrāviti*), i.e. the first triplet is in Jagatī, the last triplet in Gāyatrī, and the remaining Ṛks are in Triṣṭubh. The use of the sūkta is Laiṅgika (by the indication of the text). In the ukthya rite (the Kannada reading उक्ते क्रत्वा (*ukte kratvā*) is garbled) ⟨NOTE:60⟩, in the Maitrāvaruṇa śastra, after the anurūpa triplet, the first triplet of this sūkta is to be recited. It is stated in the sūtra: चर्षणीधृतमस्तभ्नाद्दामसुर इति तृचौ (*carṣaṇīdhṛtamastabhnāddāmasura iti tṛcau*) (Ā. 6-1). At the Viṣuvat in the niṣkevalya the triplet नृणामु त्वा (*nṛṇāmu tvā*) is used; this is stated in the Viṣuvān section: नृणामु त्वा नृतमं गीर्भिरुक्थैरिति शिस्त्रः (*nṛṇāmu tvā nṛtamaṃ gīrbhirukthairiti śistraḥ*) ⟨NOTE:61⟩ (Ā. 8-6). In the Bṛhaspatisava also this triplet is used as the nivid in the niṣkevalya; the sūtra says: नृणामु त्वैति मध्यंदिनः (*nṛṇāmu tvaiti madhyaṃdinaḥ*) (Ā. 9-5). In the Mahāvrata also this triplet is used in the niṣkevalya.

The wishes prayed for are these: may Agni taste the oblations offered by the sacrificers; grant food to the sacrificers; provide bright foods easily; conquer the sacrificers' enemies; be gracious towards the sacrificers; and grant that rites such as the Agnihotra be accomplished without obstacle.

text: Of the world of heaven, भुवा ऊधः निदधे—तत्रत्यं जलवादाय स्वकीयं मेघरूपं ऊधः उदकेन निहितमकरोत् । (*bhuvā ūdhaḥ nidadhe—tatratyaṃ jalavādāya svakīyaṃ megharūpaṃ ūdhaḥ udakena nihitamakarot |*) Gathering the waters that are on the earth, she makes her udder, which is in the form of cloud, full of sap. Afterwards, when the rainy season arrives, इळा ऋतस्य पयसा अपिन्वत (*iḷā ṛtasya payasā apinvata*): the earth is drenched with waters from the side of Āditya, who is of the nature of truth. Having explained the meaning thus, he cites the Manu-smṛti text आदित्याज्ञायते वृष्टिः वृष्टेरन्नं ततः प्रजाः (*ādityājñāyate vṛṣṭiḥ vṛṣṭerannaṃ tataḥ prajāḥ*) (Manu. 3-17): from Āditya comes rain, from rain food, and from food the creatures. ⟨NOTE:120⟩ Thus, because Heaven and Earth are engaged in the origin and so on of the worlds, the might of the gods is explained as unequalled.

text: निरित्येष समित्येतस्य स्थाने (*nirityeṣa samityetasya sthāne*) (Ni. 12-2). The prefix niḥ is used in the sense of sam. Saṃskṛta means a place that has been refined. But "refined" here may be an arrangement made so that a dwelling-place is a place of assignation and secret. The author of the Nirukta, citing the Ṛk यदादीध्ये न दविषाण्येभिः परायध्योऽव हीये सखिभ्यः । न्युप्ताश्च बभ्रवो वाचमक्रत्र एमीदेषां निष्कृतं जारिणीव ॥ (*yadādīdhye na daviṣāṇyebhiḥ parāyadhyo 'va hīye sakhibhyaḥ | nyuptāśca babhravo vācamakratra emīdeṣāṃ niṣkṛtaṃ jāriṇīva ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-34-) ⟨NOTE:194⟩, has shown that there the word niṣkṛta means a place of tryst. A woman of loose conduct going to the niṣkṛta and joining him means going to a secret place and meeting him.
